name: Sweet potatoes
tile_uses: Tacos, rice bowls, a weeknight dinner on their own
why_now: California's sweet potatoes are dug in September and October, most of them in the Central Valley around Merced, then stored through the winter. The new crop is on shelves now. It's the basket's filling one: a starch that keeps for weeks and makes a dinner on its own.
how_to_choose: Firm from end to end, with no soft or wet tips
Smooth skin, no sprouts or wrinkling
Medium and evenly shaped, so they cook at one speed
buy_this_much: 2 lbs, about four medium. They keep, so they're the dinner you make when the week gets away from you.
price_note: Cheap now, and cheaper still by the loose pound than in bags.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted in cubes
flavor_paths.description: Small, oiled, 425°F until the edges char. For tacos and bowls.

flavor_paths.name: Baked whole
flavor_paths.description: Split open, salted yogurt, ajvar. A whole dinner in one potato.

flavor_paths.name: With something sharp
flavor_paths.description: Pomegranate or lime over the top. It needs the contrast.

weekday_uses: Roasted cubes in tacos with black beans and cotija
Baked whole, split, with yogurt and a spoonful of ajvar
In a rice bowl, in place of the kabocha
Roasted cubes under a fried egg
weekend_use: A tray of roasted cubes beside the fish, for anyone who wants something warm and filling.
storage: Somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge — cold makes the centers hard and off-tasting. They keep three weeks or more.
one_thing_to_learn: A baked sweet potato is done well after it's merely soft. Keep going — an hour at 400°F — until the skin puffs away from the flesh and syrup starts to bead out and caramelize on the pan. That's the starch turning to sugar, and it's the difference between a vegetable and a meal.
